props.title: Food Matters

sections.content: Food Matters (2008) launched a wave of hard-hitting food industry documentaries that exposed troubling truths about nutrition and healthcare. Following the path blazed by Super Size Me (2004), this Australian documentary tackled the pharmaceutical industry's grip on medical education and the powerful healing potential of proper nutrition. The film shares DNA with later exposés like Fed Up (2014) and What the Health (2017), focusing on how food choices directly impact chronic disease rates.

sections.content: The movement gained serious momentum with Fed Up (2014), produced by Katie Couric, which specifically targeted the sugar industry's influence on American health policy. This sparked a series of nutrition documentaries including In Defense of Food (2015) and Sustainable (2016) that moved beyond just criticism to explore solutions. These films share a common thread of advocating for whole foods and questioning industrial food production methods.

The conversation evolved further with Rotten (2018), Netflix's investigative series that dug into food supply corruption, and Kiss the Ground (2020), which connected food production to climate change. Unlike early "shock docs" that relied heavily on grotesque footage of factory farms, these newer films take a more solutions-oriented approach while maintaining their activist edge. sections.content: Recent food documentaries have shifted from pure exposé to exploring viable alternatives. The Biggest Little Farm (2018) chronicles the eight-year quest of two urban dwellers to create a sustainable farm. Chef's Table (2015-2019) showcases chefs who prioritize local, sustainable ingredients while creating world-class cuisine. This evolution reflects growing public awareness and demand for actionable solutions to our food system challenges.
